It was asserted that deceased Shabbir Mohammed, who was 21 years of age, working under the respondent Nos.1 to 3 therein has died on 07.04.2008 while lifting a generator at the tower situated at the house of Ramesh Shastri for the present appellant, i.e. BSNL.

For the purpose of installation of generator, for the tower in question, a contract was given by the appellant-BSNL to Aditya Mathur M/s Nice Diesel Engine Pvt. Ltd. - respondent No.1 therein, who had further subcontracted the tender in favour of Rais - S/o Mohammed Rafik - respondent No.2 therein.
It was averred that the deceased was engaged by Rais for the principal employer i.e. BSNL for the purpose of installation of generator and lifting of the same at the site in question.
It was further averred that when the deceased was connecting generator with the wire, he fell down and thereafter he was taken to the hospital, where he succumbed to the injuries.

It was further averred that the deceased used to earn Rs.200/- per day as wages and was in the employment of the principal employer i.e. BSNL and that the accident took place during the course of employment.

The claimants further submitted that they had initially registered an inquest report and, thereafter, given notice to the respondents, including the present appellant, however, no compensation was paid.
Therefore, they had filed the claim application before the authority concerned.

5. The learned Commissioner thereafter proceeded to adjudicate the matter and decided all the issues in favour of the claimants and awarded the sum as stated (supra) towards compensation and other heads.
6. Being aggrieved against the same, the present appeal has been filed by the appellants.

Arguments on behalf of appellants:-
7. While challenging the impugned award, learned counsel for the appellants submitted that issue No.1 goes to the core of the matter as the appellant, being a Central Government undertaking, the learned Commissioner had no jurisdiction to entertain the claim.
Secondly, the accident having occurred at Kekadi, Ajmer, so the learned Commissioner at Nagaur had no territorial jurisdiction to entertain the claim application.

However, in order to buttress his argument, he was not in a position to place on record any document or to show any law with regard to the appellant corporation being a Central Government undertaking, there was a specific embargo with regard to the entertainment of the claim by the learned Commissioner concerned.

Learned counsel for the appellants further submitted that all the claimants do not fall within the definition of "dependent" under the Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923, and, therefore, the learned Commissioner had committed an error of law while entertaining the claim on their behalf, inasmuch as, the unmarried minor brothers and sisters were treated as dependents.

8. Learned counsel for the appellants further submitted that the appellant No.1 was not the principal employer and the principal employer was the respondent No.8-Rais and, therefore, the liability could not be fastened upon the appellant.
Learned counsel further raised an objection with regard to the amount of interest awarded, inasmuch as, interest at the rate of 12% per annum was awarded.
As per learned counsel for the appellants, the interest was on the higher side and interest not more than 9% should have been awarded by the learned Commissioner.
He, therefore, prayed for quashing and setting aside the award in question.
9. Nobody has put in appearance on behalf of the respondents.
Analysis:-

10. As far as the jurisdiction with regard to the place where the claim can be filed is concerned,
Section 21 of the Act of 1923 deals with the issue in hand and sub-section (1) of the same provides as under:-
" 21. Venue of proceedings and transfer.-

[(1) Where any matter under this Act is to be done by or before a Commissioner, the same shall, subject to the provisions of this Act and to any rules made hereunder, be done by or before the Commissioner for the area in which-- (a) the accident took place which resulted in the injury; or (b) the [employee] or in case of his death, the dependant claiming the compensation ordinarily resides; or (c) the employer has his registered office:
Provided that no matter shall be processed before or by a Commissioner, other than the Commissioner having jurisdiction over the area in which the accident took place,
without giving notice in the manner prescribed by the Central Government to the Commissioner having jurisdiction over the area and the State Government concerned:

Provided further that, where the [employee], being the master of a ship or a seaman or the captain or a member of the crew of an aircraft or [an employee] in a motor vehicle or a company, meets with the accident outside India any such matter may be done by or before a Commissioner for the area in which the owner or agent of the ship, aircraft or motor vehicle resides or carries on business or the registered office of the company is situate, as the case may be."
(Uploaded on 13/03/2026 at 11:00:46 AM) [2026:RJ-JD:11186] (7 of 9)
[CMA-124/2013]
Bsnl And Anr vs Munshi Khan And Ors. ... on 6 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/63900823/
4 11.

A bare perusal of clause (b) of Sub-Section (1) of Section 21 of the Act of 1923 itself reveals that a claim can be filed at the place where the employee, or in case of his death, the dependent claiming the compensation ordinarily resides.

In the present case, the claimants are admittedly residing at Nagaur and, therefore, in view of the specific provision of Section 21 of the Act of 1923, the learned Commissioner was having the jurisdiction and has rightly entertained the claim application and adjudicated the same.

12. As regards the first argument raised by the learned counsel for the appellants with regard to appellant No.1 being a Government of India undertaking and the learned Commissioner not having jurisdiction in this regard, it is needless to emphasize that no such law or provision has been shown whereby there is any specific embargo with regard to entertaining of such claim.

Secondly, even as per the conditions of the contract entered between the appellant No.1 and the respondent No.7 Aditya Mathur, a bare perusal of Clause 18 reveals that there is a specific reference to any claim being decided by the learned Commissioner under the Act of 1923, qua which, recovery can be made by the appellant No.1 from the contractor.
Therefore, the argument raised by learned counsel for the appellants falls flat and has rightly been rejected by the learned Commissioner.

13. As regards the second ground raised by learned counsel for the appellants with regard to dependents of the deceased are concerned, a bare perusal of the Section 2 sub-section iii(d) of the Act of 1923 reveals that even a minor brother, unmarried sister, or even a widowed sister, if minor,
fall within the definition of "dependent".
In the present case, firstly, no such objection was taken by the appellants before the learned Commissioner and such objection cannot be permitted to be raised for the first time before this Court.

Even otherwise, the appellants have not been able to show that respondent Nos.4 to 6 do not fall within the definition of "dependent" in view of the specific definition provided under the Act of 1923.

15. As far as the third objection taken by the learned counsel for the appellants is concerned, it is needless to emphasize that an appeal under Section 30 of the Act 1923 can be entertained only if substantial question of law is involved.
As far as the rate of interest is concerned, the same can hardly be said to give rise to a substantial question of law.
Even otherwise, the rate of interest awarded by the learned Commissioner is in consonance with the provisions of the Act and cannot be said to be excessive or arbitrary.

16. The fourth ground raised by the learned counsel for the appellants was with regard to there being no employer-employee relationship between the appellants and the deceased, as the contract entered between the appellants was with respondent No.7 - Aditya Mathur and not with the deceased.

17. As far as the argument in question is concerned, a bare perusal of definition of "employer"
provided under Section 2(e) of the Act

reveals the same, which provides as under:-
Bsnl And Anr vs Munshi Khan And Ors. ... on 6 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/63900823/
5 "Section 2(e) - "employer" includes any body of persons whether incorporated or not and any managing agent of an employer and the legal representative of a deceased employer, and, when the services of [an employee] are temporarily lent or let on hire to another person by the person with whom the [employee] has entered into a contract of service or apprenticeship, means such other person while the [employee]
is working for him;"

sentences.text: (Uploaded on 13/03/2026 at 11:00:46 AM)

18. A bare perusal of the aforesaid provision reveals that, even if, the work is given through a contractor by the principal employer, then too, the employer engaged by such contractor or even employed as an apprentice is to be treated as an employee of the principal employer.

Thus, in view of the definition as stated (supra), the argument of the learned counsel for the appellants does not hold any substance, more particularly, where there is an admission on the part of the appellants that the generator was to be installed on their behalf based upon the contract given to respondent No.7 - Aditya Mathur for the purpose of functioning of the tower in question.
19. Thus, the facts of the present case clearly fortify the fact that the appellant No.1 was the principal employer.
The learned Commissioner has thus, rightly considered this aspect of the matter while passing the impunged award.
20. As an upshot of the above discussion, the appeal filed by the appellant is bereft of merit and does not involve any substantial question of law.
The same is, therefore, dismissed.
21. All pending applications also stand disposed of.

(SANDEEP SHAH),J 24-Love/-
